summary: Lists software tools that can be used to test and evaluate TCP implementations, or that give specific results about how a TCP behaves. It is a pointer document for implementors who want to check their stack, not a protocol specification. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you built a toy car, you would want ways to test how well it drives. This is a list of tools for testing how well a computer handles its internet conversations.

questions: what tools can test a tcp implementation
how do i test tcp implementations
how do i test if my tcp is correct
subtitle: A guide to software tools that test how well TCP implementations follow the specification.

tldr.problem: TCP implementations in many operating systems and devices need to be tested to ensure they follow the RFC 793 specification correctly and perform well. Without testing tools, implementors cannot evaluate their TCP stack or compare different implementations.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs 12 testing tools in three categories: functional correctness tools that check if a TCP follows the specification, performance tools that measure speed and throughput, and stress tools that test behavior under high load.
tldr.outcome: Developers can choose appropriate tools to validate their TCP implementations, test edge cases, and optimize performance. Better testing has led to more compatible and reliable TCP implementations across operating systems.

facts.label: Supported platforms
facts.value: BSD, Linux, Solaris, HP-UX, IRIX, Windows

today: RFC 2398 is an Informational RFC published in August 1998. The specific tools listed are no longer in active use in their original forms, as some (like dummynet) have been superseded by modern equivalents. However, the categories and approaches—simulating network conditions, injecting faults, capturing and analyzing traces, measuring throughput—remain fundamental to TCP testing. Modern testing frameworks like eBPF-based tools, container-based network emulation, and cloud network simulation tools have evolved from these roots. The need to test TCP implementations rigorously remains just as critical today as in 1998.

sections.title: Introduction to TCP Testing
sections.content:
RFC 2398 is a catalog of publicly available software tools for testing TCP implementations. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the most widely used protocol for reliable data transmission on the internet, but the specification in RFC 793 is complex, and different operating systems have implemented it in different ways.

This memo lists tools in three categories. Functional correctness tools check whether an implementation follows the RFC specification precisely: Does it handle retransmission correctly? Does it implement the congestion window properly? Performance tools measure how fast TCP can send and receive data, and how efficiently it uses CPU. Stress tools test how TCP behaves under extreme load, with thousands of packets per second or network congestion.

The RFC emphasizes that this is not an exhaustive list, but rather documents tools that were verified as available and in use within the TCP Implementers working group of the IETF. For each tool, the memo describes what the tool does, how difficult it is to set up and run, how to obtain it, and what computing environment it requires.
sections.eli5: This is like a shopping catalog of test tools. Each tool is good for different kinds of testing: checking that TCP works right, checking that it is fast, or checking that it does not break under heavy traffic.

sections.title: Overview of Testing Tools
sections.content:
The RFC describes 12 tools spanning a range of approaches and platforms.

Dbs (Performance/Stress) coordinates multiple data transfers and logs the results. Dummynet (Functional/Performance) is a BSD kernel module that simulates network delays, bandwidth limits, and queue constraints between protocol layers, allowing tests on the same machine.

Netperf (Performance) is a classic bandwidth benchmark tool that measures single-connection throughput and latency for TCP, UDP, and DLPI, with support for CPU utilization measurement. NIST Net (Functional/Performance) is a Linux kernel patch that turns a machine into a configurable router, introducing realistic network conditions like packet loss, delays, and congestion.

Orchestra (Functional/Performance) is a sophisticated tool that sits inside the protocol stack and can inject faults—drop packets, delay them, reorder them, or modify them—based on configurable Tcl scripts. This allows targeting specific TCP behaviors. Packet Shell (Functional/Performance) is a Tcl/Tk-based framework for building and manipulating network packets, with dynamic protocol libraries for IP, TCP, UDP, ICMP and others.

Tcpanaly (Functional/Performance) analyzes TCP behavior by inspecting packet traces. It can determine which TCP implementation the trace came from and identify deviations from expected behavior. Tcptrace (Functional/Performance) is a trace analysis tool that reads tcpdump output and produces detailed statistics and graphs showing segment transmission, acknowledgments, and round-trip times.

Tracelook (Functional/Performance) provides a graphical interface for inspecting tcpdump traces, plotting variables like advertised window and sequence numbers. TReno (Performance) measures TCP throughput by simulating TCP's congestion control using UDP packets, allowing throughput measurement without relying on the TCP implementation under test.

Ttcp (Performance) is a simple throughput benchmark tool and traffic generator, available in many variants. Xplot (Functional/Performance) is a graphing tool that visualizes TCP behavior from tcpdump traces, particularly the classic time-sequence plots that show segment transmission and acknowledgment timing.
sections.eli5: Some tools count how fast TCP sends data (Netperf, Ttcp). Some break the network on purpose to see if TCP notices (Dummynet, NIST Net). Some read recordings of what TCP did and analyze them (Tcptrace, Tcpanaly). Some draw pictures of TCP's behavior over time (Xplot).

sections.title: Tool Categories and Selection
sections.content:
Choosing a tool depends on what you need to test. For functional correctness, you want tools that can inject faults and see if TCP detects them, or tools that can analyze traces and spot deviations from the spec. Orchestra and Dummynet are powerful for this because they can simulate realistic network failures. Tcpanaly is powerful because it has built-in knowledge of many TCP implementations and can diagnose discrepancies.

For performance testing, simple tools like Netperf or Ttcp suffice if you just need throughput and latency numbers. Tools like Dummynet and NIST Net are also useful for measuring performance under network stress. The trace-analysis tools (Tcptrace, Xplot) help you visualize performance characteristics like congestion response.

For stress testing, you want tools that can generate high packet rates or introduce severe network conditions. Dummynet and NIST Net can inject high loss rates and delays. Dbs can coordinate many simultaneous transfers.

Some tools require deep operating-system-level changes (Dummynet and NIST Net require kernel modifications), while others run as user-level applications. Some require source code changes to TCP itself (Packet Shell), while others work with unmodified implementations (Tcpanaly on packet traces). The memo notes that any tool requiring kernel modifications or running as root deserves scrutiny, since foreign code could contain malicious payloads.
sections.eli5: If you want to know if TCP works right, use tools that break things and see if TCP handles it. If you want to know if TCP is fast, use speed-measuring tools. If you want to know if it survives chaos, stress it with lots of broken packets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Network testing tools present security risks that developers should understand. Some tools can create rogue packets or launch denial-of-service attacks. Many require root privileges or kernel modifications, meaning you are trusting code from a potentially untrustworthy source with deep access to your system. A malicious tool could contain code that logs traffic, modifies packets, or compromises the system.

Additionally, tools that capture network traffic (like tcpdump, used by trace-analysis tools) can read other people's traffic on the local network segment, potentially exposing passwords, data, and private information. These tools should be run only in controlled lab environments, never on production or shared networks.

None of the tools listed evaluate the security of TCP itself (whether TCP is resistant to denial-of-service attacks, for example). They test functional correctness and performance, not security properties.
sections.eli5: These are powerful tools that can see and change network traffic, so only use them in a lab where you control the network. Do not run them on a network with sensitive data or other people's computers, and be careful about downloading tools from untrusted sources.
